newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hani killer accused of hiding SAfrican accomplices.
newsitem.headline: Hani killer accused of hiding SAfrican accomplices.

text.p: A white rightist who killed South African communist leader Chris Hani was accused on Tuesday of withholding evidence that others knew of the plot in advance.

Far-right Conservative Party politician Clive Derby-Lewis, who supplied the gun that killed Hani, and Janusz Walus, the Polish immigrant who pulled the trigger, are seeking amnesty for the assassination over the 1993 Easter weekend.
In papers supporting their amnesty request, the pair said they planned and executed the killing without outside help.

But lawyer George Bizos, who is opposing amnesty on behalf of the Hani family, handed in a statement by another right-winger, a Mr N.J. Visser, which he said suggested that other rightists had prior knowledge of the plot.
"It would appear Mr Visser knew about the plan to kill Mr Hani," he said in his cross-examination of Derby-Lewis.
"You did not act alone with Mr Walus, but you acted together with your wife and a number of other people," Bizos said to Derby-Lewis, who denied the accusation.
His Australian wife Gaye was acquitted of the murder in their criminal trial. She cannot be tried again.
Visser is also seeking amnesty from the statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission for stealing money from a pension fund to buy equipment for right-wing paramilitary groups.
In his statement, he said he had opposed Hani's killing.
"I personally was against the murder of Mr Hani because we had information that Hani and Winnie Mandela wanted to establish their own political party," he said.
"This would be in our interests because the youth would vote for them rather than the ANC."

Walus, a communist-hater since his childhood in Poland, is unlikely to testify this week. Truth commission lawyer Mokotedi Mpshe told reporters the hearing would be postponed at the weekend until November to hear further evidence.
